title: Architecture: Form, Space, and Order
why: The drawing-led primer most schools set in first year: points, lines, planes, volumes and how they organise space.

title: 101 Things I Learned in Architecture School
why: One lesson per page, each with a sketch. The quickest way to hear what studio tutors keep saying.

title: Experiencing Architecture
why: How buildings feel to walk through: solids and cavities, scale, rhythm, texture, daylight, colour and sound.

title: The Eyes of the Skin
why: A short argument that architecture is for all the senses, not just the eye. Read in one sitting.

title: Thinking Architecture
why: Short essays on how buildings feel: material, sound, light and the memory of places. By the architect of Therme Vals.

title: Atmospheres
why: Nine things that make a building feel the way it does, from a lecture Zumthor gave in a garden.

title: Lessons for Students in Architecture
why: Hertzberger shows his own buildings and others to explain thresholds, in-between spaces and how people take over a place.

title: Analysing Architecture
why: How to read a building: the basic elements, the way they frame places, and drawings that show it.

title: Precedents in Architecture
by: Roger H. Clark and Michael Pause
why: Dozens of famous buildings redrawn as the same set of diagrams: structure, light, circulation, geometry. Learn how to analyse precedents.

title: The Place of Houses
by: Charles Moore, Gerald Allen and Donlyn Lyndon
why: How a house makes rooms, machines and dreams fit together. Plain, warm and still useful for a first house project.

title: Architecture: A Very Short Introduction
why: What architecture is for, in a hundred pages. Good before the first lecture.

title: Why Architecture Matters
why: A critic explains why buildings move us, without jargon.

title: The Architecture of Happiness
why: Why some rooms make us feel at home and others do not. A popular book that gets students talking about taste.

title: How Buildings Learn
why: What happens to buildings after the architect leaves: layers that change at different speeds.

title: Body, Memory, and Architecture
by: Kent C. Bloomer and Charles W. Moore
why: How the body and memory shape the way we experience buildings. A short classic from Yale.

title: Learning from Las Vegas
by: Robert Venturi, Denise Scott Brown and Steven Izenour
why: The studio that went to the Strip and came back with the duck and the decorated shed.

title: Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture
why: "Less is a bore." The gentle manifesto that opened the door to postmodernism.

title: Delirious New York
why: A retroactive manifesto for Manhattan: the grid, the skyscraper and the culture of congestion.

title: S,M,L,XL
why: Projects, essays and diary entries sorted by size. The book that made the architecture monograph big.

title: The Architecture of the City
why: The city as a collective memory built from types and monuments. Key to reading European urban form.

title: Genius Loci: Towards a Phenomenology of Architecture
why: The spirit of a place, and how buildings can belong to it.

title: The Poetics of Space
why: A philosopher on cellars, attics, drawers and nests: the house as a place of the imagination.

title: In Praise of Shadows
why: A short Japanese essay on darkness, lacquer, paper and the beauty of dim rooms.

title: Invisible Cities
why: Marco Polo describes fifty-five imaginary cities to Kublai Khan. Fiction that every studio quotes.

title: The Hidden Dimension
why: How much space people need, and how it differs between cultures. The origin of proxemics.

title: Words and Buildings: A Vocabulary of Modern Architecture
why: Where words like form, space, structure and truth came from, and what architects mean by them.

title: Architecture and Disjunction
why: Essays on event, movement and violence in space, from the architect of Parc de la Villette.

title: The Language of Post-Modern Architecture
why: The book that named postmodernism, and famously dated the death of modern architecture to 1972.

title: Deconstructivist Architecture
why: The MoMA show that put Gehry, Hadid, Libeskind, Koolhaas, Eisenman, Tschumi and Coop Himmelb(l)au in one room.

title: The Autopoiesis of Architecture
why: The theory behind parametricism, by the partner who ran Zaha Hadid Architects after her.

title: Digital Culture in Architecture
why: What computers changed in how architecture is thought, drawn and built.

title: Architecture Depends
why: Architecture is messy, contingent and shaped by everyone else. An argument against the lone genius.

title: Spatial Agency: Other Ways of Doing Architecture
by: Nishat Awan, Tatjana Schneider and Jeremy Till
why: A catalogue of people who make space without being a conventional architect.

title: Thermal Delight in Architecture
why: Warmth and coolness as things to design with, not just to control. Slim and loved.

title: The Craftsman
why: On making things well, and what skilled work does to the maker.

title: Architecture Without Architects
why: Villages, caves and cities built by nobody famous. A picture book that widened the subject.

title: Towards a New Architecture
why: Ships, aeroplanes, grain silos and the five points. The loudest book of the twentieth century.

title: The City of To-morrow and Its Planning
why: Le Corbusier proposes to flatten the centre of Paris for towers in a park. Read it to argue with it.

title: Ornament and Crime
why: The essay that declared decoration a crime, and the plain white wall a sign of culture.

title: The New Architecture and the Bauhaus
why: Gropius explains what the Bauhaus was trying to do, in his own words.

title: The International Style
why: The MoMA catalogue that turned European modernism into a style with three rules.

title: The New Brutalism: Ethic or Aesthetic?
why: Banham on the Smithsons and the movement he helped name, with the buildings as they were new.

title: Metabolism in Architecture
why: Capsules, megastructures and cities that grow like organisms, from the Metabolist who built Nakagin.

title: Yes Is More: An Archicomic on Architectural Evolution
why: BIG's projects told as a comic strip. Pragmatic, optimistic and very easy to read.

title: A Pattern Language
by: Christopher Alexander, Sara Ishikawa and Murray Silverstein
why: 253 patterns, from regions to window seats, each a problem and a solution. Open it anywhere.

title: The Timeless Way of Building
why: The quality without a name, and why old towns have it. The theory behind A Pattern Language.

title: Elements of Architecture
why: Floor, wall, ceiling, roof, door, window, stair, lift, ramp, toilet, fireplace, corridor, balcony. Each element gets its own history.

title: Modern Architecture Since 1900
why: The standard survey of the modern movement worldwide, with the buildings on this wall in it.

title: Modern Architecture: A Critical History
why: Denser than Curtis and more argued. The other book every history course sets.

title: Space, Time and Architecture
why: The first great history of modern architecture, written while it was happening.

title: The Classical Language of Architecture
why: The orders, the rules and how architects bent them, in six short radio talks.

title: A History of Architecture on the Comparative Method
why: The big reference with the famous comparative plates. Still on every library shelf.

title: The Future of Architecture, Since 1889
why: A newer world survey that gives Latin America, Asia and Africa their place.

title: A Global History of Architecture
by: Francis D. K. Ching, Mark Jarzombek and Vikramaditya Prakash
why: Buildings from every continent, arranged by date rather than by country, with Ching drawings.

title: Theory and Design in the First Machine Age
why: Where the ideas of modernism came from: futurism, De Stijl, the Bauhaus and the machine.

title: The Architecture of the Well-tempered Environment
why: A history of heating, lighting and ventilation, and how services shaped modern buildings.

title: Bauhaus 1919–1933
why: The school, the teachers, the workshops and the building, in one well-illustrated volume.

title: Brunelleschi's Dome
why: How the dome of Florence cathedral was built without centering. History that reads like a story.

title: The Mosque: History, Architectural Development and Regional Diversity
why: Mosques from Cordoba to Isfahan to Dhaka, by region and period.

title: This Brutal World
why: Concrete buildings from around the world in black and white photographs.

title: SOS Brutalism: A Global Survey
by: Oliver Elser, Philip Kurz and Peter Cachola Schmal (editors)
why: A survey of brutalist buildings worldwide and the campaign to save them.

title: Raw Concrete: The Beauty of Brutalism
why: Eight British brutalist buildings visited and explained by someone who loves them.

title: Project Japan: Metabolism Talks
by: Rem Koolhaas and Hans Ulrich Obrist
why: Interviews with the surviving Metabolists, with the drawings and the politics behind them.

title: Where Are the Women Architects?
why: Why so few women are remembered in architecture, and what is changing.

title: Louis I. Kahn
why: Kahn's buildings described one by one, with plans and photographs. The best single volume on him.

title: Louis Kahn: Essential Texts
by: Louis I. Kahn, edited by Robert Twombly
why: Kahn in his own words: silence and light, served and servant, what a brick wants to be.

title: Between Silence and Light: Spirit in the Architecture of Louis I. Kahn
why: Kahn's sayings set against photographs of his buildings. Short and often given as a gift.

title: An Autobiography
why: Wright tells his own story, with the prairie, the Taliesins and the ideas behind organic architecture.

title: Le Corbusier: Ideas and Forms
why: The whole career, from La Chaux-de-Fonds to Chandigarh, with the ideas explained.

title: Mies van der Rohe: A Critical Biography
why: The life behind the glass boxes, from Berlin to Chicago.

title: Alvar Aalto
why: Aalto's buildings explained with plans and sections. Good on why they feel humane.

title: Carlo Scarpa
why: The Venetian master of the joint and the detail, building by building.

title: Luis Barragán: The Complete Works
why: Walls, water and colour in Mexico. The standard book on Barragán.

title: Tadao Ando: Complete Works
why: Ando's concrete, light and geometry, with his own essays.

title: The Curves of Time: The Memoirs of Oscar Niemeyer
why: Niemeyer on Brasília, curves, communism and a long life.

title: Utzon: Inspiration, Vision, Architecture
why: From Sydney to Bagsværd and Can Lis, the big book on Utzon.

title: Gaudí: The Complete Buildings
why: Every Gaudí building photographed, with the structural ideas behind the shapes.

title: Herzog & de Meuron: Natural History
why: The Canadian Centre for Architecture catalogue on how the practice thinks about materials and surfaces.

title: Álvaro Siza: Complete Works
why: White walls in the Portuguese landscape, with Frampton explaining what makes Siza careful.

title: Anti-Object: The Dissolution and Disintegration of Architecture
why: Kuma argues against buildings as objects, for buildings that dissolve into their places.

title: Shigeru Ban: Complete Works 1985–2010
why: Paper tubes, timber grids and emergency shelters, in one large book.

title: Conversations with Frank Gehry
why: Gehry talks about Bilbao, Disney Hall and how he works.

title: Renzo Piano: Logbook
why: Piano's projects as a journal, with sketches, from the Pompidou on.

title: Norman Foster: A Life in Architecture
why: The biography of the high-tech architect who became a global practice.

title: I. M. Pei: Complete Works
by: Philip Jodidio and Janet Adams Strong
why: From the Louvre pyramid to Suzhou, with Pei involved in the book.

title: Lina Bo Bardi
by: Zeuler R. M. de A. Lima
why: The Italian-Brazilian architect of MASP and SESC Pompéia, finally with a full study.

title: Charles and Ray Eames: Designers of the Twentieth Century
why: Furniture, films and the house in Pacific Palisades, by the historian who knew Ray.

title: Sverre Fehn: The Pattern of Thoughts
why: The Norwegian master of the Nordic Pavilion and Hedmark Museum, by a former student.

title: Sigurd Lewerentz, Architect
why: The brick churches at Klippan and Björkhagen and the Woodland Cemetery, by the architect who worked with him.

title: Francis Kéré: Radically Simple
why: Schools and clinics in Burkina Faso built with clay, community and very little money.

title: Architecture for the Poor
why: Fathy builds a village in mud brick at New Gourna and writes down what he learnt.

title: Geoffrey Bawa: The Complete Works
why: Tropical modernism in Sri Lanka: courtyards, verandas and gardens.

title: Architectural Graphics
why: Plans, sections, elevations, paraline and perspective drawings, and how to letter them.

title: A Visual Dictionary of Architecture
why: Every term a student meets, each with a drawing. Keep it on the desk.

title: Drawing for Architecture
why: Krier's polemical cartoons on cities, towers and taste. You will disagree, and learn to draw an argument.

title: Manual of Section
by: Paul Lewis, Marc Tsurumaki and David J. Lewis
why: Sixty-three buildings redrawn in section at the same scale, and seven kinds of section explained.

title: Operative Design: A Catalogue of Spatial Verbs
by: Anthony Di Mari and Nora Yoo
why: Extrude, lift, carve, nest: form-making moves as small diagrams. Useful in the first weeks of a project.

title: Freehand Drawing and Discovery
why: Quick sketching on site and in the studio, with the pen tricks that make it look easy.

title: Building Construction Illustrated
why: Foundations, walls, floors, roofs and openings, drawn so you can see how they go together.

title: Architectural Graphic Standards
by: Charles George Ramsey and Harold Reeve Sleeper
why: The American reference of dimensions and details that offices have used for ninety years.

title: Constructing Architecture: Materials, Processes, Structures
why: The ETH Zurich handbook: materials, elements and whole buildings, with superb drawings.

title: Structures: Or Why Things Don't Fall Down
why: Tension, compression, beams and arches explained with humour and no heavy maths.

title: Studies in Tectonic Culture
why: How the way a building is put together carries its meaning, from Semper to Kahn, Scarpa and Utzon.

title: Brick: A World History
by: James W. P. Campbell and Will Pryce
why: Five thousand years of brick, superbly photographed.

title: Concrete and Culture: A Material History
why: Why concrete is loved and hated, and what it has meant in different places.

title: Sun, Wind & Light: Architectural Design Strategies
by: G. Z. Brown and Mark DeKay
why: Climate-responsive design as rules of thumb you can use at sketch stage.

title: Cradle to Cradle: Remaking the Way We Make Things
why: Design so that waste becomes food. The book that started many sustainability arguments.

title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
why: Sidewalks, mixed uses, old buildings and eyes on the street. The book that stopped the bulldozers.

title: The Image of the City
why: Paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks: how people hold a city in their heads.

title: Life Between Buildings
why: What makes people stop, sit and stay in public space. Short and practical.

title: Cities for People
why: Gehl at the end of his career, with the Copenhagen lessons applied to the world.

title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
why: Whyte filmed New York plazas to see where people sit. Sun, seats, water, food, and other people.

title: Collage City
why: Against the total plan: the city as a collage of fragments and figure-ground.

title: Garden Cities of To-morrow
why: The three magnets and the garden city. The start of modern town planning.

title: The Mathematics of the Ideal Villa and Other Essays
why: Palladio and Le Corbusier side by side, and other essays that taught architects to compare plans.

title: Design with Nature
why: Layer the maps of soil, water and slope before you draw. The start of ecological planning.

title: The Landscape of Man
why: Gardens and landscapes from prehistory to today, around the world.

title: The Granite Garden: Urban Nature and Human Design
why: The city as a natural system: air, earth, water, life.

title: The New Landscape: Urbanisation in the Third World
why: Correa on Bombay, housing and the city that most of the world's people actually live in.

title: A Place in the Shade: The New Landscape and Other Essays
why: Correa's essays on open-to-sky space, climate and Indian cities, collected late in his life.

title: Charles Correa
why: Correa's buildings, from Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya to Jawahar Kala Kendra, with Frampton's reading of them.

title: Laurie Baker: Life, Work, Writings
why: The Kerala architect of cheap brick, rat-trap bonds and jali walls, with his own writings.

title: Paths Uncharted
why: Doshi's own account of working with Le Corbusier and Kahn and building Sangath and Aranya.

title: Balkrishna Doshi: Architecture for the People
by: Mateo Kries, Khushnu Panthaki Hoof and Jolanthe Kugler (editors)
why: The Vitra Design Museum catalogue for the Pritzker year, with the projects well photographed.

title: Indian Architecture (Buddhist and Hindu Periods)
why: The old survey of temples, stupas and caves that Indian schools still set.

title: Architecture of Mughal India
why: From Babur to Aurangzeb: forts, tombs, mosques and gardens, with their patrons.

title: The Ten Books on Architecture
why: Firmness, commodity and delight. The only architecture book to survive from antiquity, free online.

title: The Four Books of Architecture
why: Palladio's villas and the orders, drawn by himself. Public domain, and the plates are online.

title: The Seven Lamps of Architecture
why: Sacrifice, truth, power, beauty, life, memory and obedience: Ruskin on what buildings owe us.

title: The Stones of Venice
why: Venice building by building, and the famous chapter on the nature of Gothic.

title: Jean Nouvel: Complete Works 1970–2008
why: Nouvel's buildings from the Institut du Monde Arabe onward, with plans and photographs.

title: Santiago Calatrava: Complete Works 1979–2009
why: Bridges, stations and museums by the engineer-architect, with his sketches of bodies and birds.

title: Japan-ness in Architecture
why: Isozaki asks what makes architecture Japanese, from Ise and Katsura to Tange.

title: Arata Isozaki
why: Isozaki's long career, from Metabolism to Postmodernism and beyond, building by building.

title: Richard Meier, Architect
why: Meier's white houses and museums, with his own text on light and geometry.

title: Mario Botta
why: Botta's brick and stone geometry, from Ticino houses to cathedrals.

title: Beyond Habitat
why: Safdie tells how a student thesis became Habitat 67 in Montreal.

title: If Walls Could Speak: My Life in Architecture
why: Safdie looks back on sixty years, from Habitat 67 to Marina Bay Sands.

title: Theoretical Anxiety and Design Strategies in the Work of Eight Contemporary Architects
why: Moneo, a fine teacher, reads Stirling, Venturi, Rossi, Eisenman, Siza, Gehry, Koolhaas and Herzog & de Meuron.

title: Tarzans in the Media Forest
why: Essays on lightness, flow and the electronic city, from the architect of the Sendai Mediatheque.

title: Erich Mendelsohn: Complete Works of the Architect
why: Mendelsohn's sketches and buildings, from the Einstein Tower to his department stores.

title: Eero Saarinen: Shaping the Future
why: The TWA terminal, the Gateway Arch and the rest, in the catalogue of the big Saarinen exhibition.

title: FARMAX: Excursions on Density
why: Dutch density pushed to the limit, in diagrams and data. The book that made MVRDV.

title: KM3: Excursions on Capacities
why: A huge, playful book of experiments in stacking cities and landscapes.

title: Arne Jacobsen
why: The Danish architect of the SAS hotel and the Egg chair, with every scale from spoons to city halls.

title: Charles Rennie Mackintosh and the Modern Movement
why: The first serious study of Mackintosh and his Glasgow School of Art.

title: The City: Its Growth, Its Decay, Its Future
why: Saarinen's theory of organic decentralisation, written at Cranbrook.

title: Hans Scharoun
why: The organic modernist of the Berlin Philharmonie, explained plan by plan.

title: Anchoring
why: Holl's early houses and projects and his idea that a building should be anchored to its place.

title: Parallax
why: Holl on perception, light, water and the body moving through space.

title: Questions of Perception: Phenomenology of Architecture
by: Steven Holl, Juhani Pallasmaa and Alberto Pérez-Gómez
why: Three short essays that introduced phenomenology to a generation of students.

title: Theoretical Practice
why: Chipperfield's early work and his quiet case for permanence and restraint.

title: Modern Architecture
why: Wagner's handbook for his students in Vienna, arguing that new needs demand new forms.

title: Aesthetics and Technology in Building
why: Nervi's Harvard lectures on how structure and beauty grow from the same thinking.

title: Marcel Breuer: Design and Architecture
by: Alexander von Vegesack and Mathias Remmele (editors)
why: From the Wassily chair to the Whitney Museum, the Vitra catalogue on Breuer.

title: Zaha Hadid: The Complete Buildings and Projects
why: Hadid's paintings and early buildings, from The Peak to the Vitra Fire Station.

title: Philip Johnson: Life and Work
why: The long and controversial career of the curator, architect and taste-maker.

title: Breaking Ground: Adventures in Life and Architecture
why: Libeskind tells his own story, from Łódź to the Jewish Museum Berlin and Ground Zero.

title: Investigations in Collective Form
why: Maki proposes group form: buildings that add up to a city the way villages do.

title: Katsura: Tradition and Creation in Japanese Architecture
why: Two modernists look at the Katsura villa, with Yasuhiro Ishimoto's famous photographs.

title: The Architecture of Paul Rudolph
why: The Yale Art and Architecture Building and the rest of Rudolph’s concrete work, reconsidered.

title: James Stirling: Buildings and Projects
why: Stirling’s career from Leicester Engineering to the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart.

title: Survival Through Design
why: Neutra argues that design should serve human biology and nerves: an early call for health in buildings.

title: Can Our Cities Survive?
why: The CIAM case for the functional city, set out for American readers.

title: A Life in Architecture
why: Yamasaki on his work, including the World Trade Center and Pruitt-Igoe.

title: Spoken into the Void: Collected Essays 1897–1900
why: Loos’s sharp early essays on clothes, furniture, plumbing and taste.

title: Aldo van Eyck: Writings
why: The playgrounds, the orphanage and the in-between, in van Eyck’s own words.

title: The Manhattan Transcripts
why: Drawings that record movement and events instead of objects. A key text for diagrams.

title: Event-Cities
why: Tschumi’s competitions and projects, from Parc de la Villette on.

title: Adjaye: Africa: Architecture
why: Adjaye photographed the buildings of 53 African capitals and sorted them by terrain.

title: Finding Form: Towards an Architecture of the Minimal
why: Soap films, hanging chains and tents: how Frei Otto found forms by experiment.

title: Alpine Architecture
why: Glass cathedrals on mountain tops: Taut’s utopian drawings after the First World War.

title: Scope of Total Architecture
why: Gropius’s late essays on teaching, teamwork and the whole environment.

title: Space and the Architect: Lessons in Architecture 2
why: Hertzberger’s second book of lessons, on space that people can make their own.

title: The Modulor
why: Le Corbusier’s proportioning system based on the human body and the golden section.

title: When the Cathedrals Were White
why: Le Corbusier visits America and finds New York too small.

title: Journey to the East
why: The sketchbooks and letters of the young Le Corbusier travelling to Istanbul and Athens.

title: The Natural House
why: Wright explains the Usonian house, for people of modest means.

title: The Disappearing City
why: Wright’s case against the dense city, and the seed of Broadacre City.

title: Mies van der Rohe: The Art of Structure
why: Mies’s buildings shown through their steel frames and details, made with Mies.

title: Peter Zumthor Works: Buildings and Projects 1979–1997
why: Zumthor’s early buildings, from the Sogn Benedetg chapel to Therme Vals and Bregenz.

title: Charles Correa: Housing and Urbanisation
why: Correa’s plans for low-rise, high-density housing in India, with Navi Mumbai and Belapur.

title: Katsura Imperial Villa
why: The villa that moved Taut, Gropius and Tange, photographed and explained.

title: On the Art of Building in Ten Books
why: The Renaissance answer to Vitruvius: beauty as harmony of all the parts.

title: An Essay on Architecture
why: The primitive hut: Laugier’s argument that columns, beams and roof are all architecture needs.

title: The Four Elements of Architecture and Other Writings
why: Hearth, roof, enclosure and mound: Semper’s theory of where building comes from.

title: Contrasts
why: Pugin sets Gothic towns against modern ones, plate by plate, to argue for Gothic.

title: Discourses on Architecture
why: Viollet-le-Duc’s lectures on structural honesty, with famous drawings of iron and masonry.

title: The Grammar of Ornament
why: A hundred colour plates of ornament from every culture. Public domain and online.

title: Kindergarten Chats
why: Sullivan teaches an imaginary student, and explains form follows function.

title: The Autobiography of an Idea
why: Sullivan’s life story and the birth of the skyscraper in Chicago.

title: Architectural Principles in the Age of Humanism
why: Proportion and geometry in Alberti and Palladio. A book that changed how architects drew.

title: Pioneers of Modern Design
why: From William Morris to Walter Gropius: Pevsner’s classic origin story of modernism.

title: An Outline of European Architecture
why: European architecture from Greece to the twentieth century in one short book.

title: A History of Building Types
why: Theatres, libraries, prisons, hospitals: how each building type took its form.

title: Architecture and Utopia: Design and Capitalist Development
why: A hard, important critique of modern architecture’s dreams.

title: Los Angeles: The Architecture of Four Ecologies
why: Banham learnt to drive to read Los Angeles: beaches, foothills, plains and freeways.

title: Ten Canonical Buildings 1950–2000
why: Eisenman reads ten buildings closely, from Mies to Koolhaas, through their drawings.

title: White Walls, Designer Dresses: The Fashioning of Modern Architecture
why: Why are modern walls white? Wigley follows the paint back to fashion.

title: Privacy and Publicity: Modern Architecture as Mass Media
why: Loos, Le Corbusier and how photographs and magazines made modern architecture.

title: The Thinking Hand
why: Pallasmaa on drawing, making and the knowledge held in the hand.

title: Notes on the Synthesis of Form
why: Alexander’s first book: design as fitting a form to its context.

title: The Dynamics of Architectural Form
why: A psychologist of perception on weight, balance and order in buildings.

title: Translations from Drawing to Building and Other Essays
why: Evans shows how drawings shape what gets built. Brilliant essays.

title: Architecture and the Crisis of Modern Science
why: How architecture lost its meaning when it became a technical science.

title: A History of Architecture: Settings and Rituals
why: A world survey that reads buildings as settings for human life.

title: The City Shaped: Urban Patterns and Meanings Through History
why: Grids, organic towns, diagrams and skylines: the forms cities take and why.

title: The City Assembled
why: The parts of a city: edges, divisions, public places and streets.

title: History of Modern Architecture
why: A two-volume history of modernism that starts with the industrial city.

title: Architecture as Space
why: Zevi argues that space, not walls, is what architecture is about.

title: The City in History
why: Mumford’s great history of the city from the first villages to the suburb.

title: The Culture of Cities
why: An early, humane case for cities planned around life rather than machines.

title: The Concise Townscape
why: Serial vision, here and there, enclosure: how to see and draw a town as you walk it.

title: City Planning According to Artistic Principles
why: Sitte studies old squares to show what makes public space feel right.

title: Good City Form
why: Lynch asks what a good city is, and gives five measures for it.

title: Cities for a Small Planet
why: Rogers’s Reith Lectures on dense, green, compact cities.

title: Triumph of the City
why: An economist’s case that cities make us richer, greener and happier.

title: Home: A Short History of an Idea
why: How comfort, privacy and domesticity were invented, room by room.

title: Welcome to Your World: How the Built Environment Shapes Our Lives
why: Cognitive science on how buildings and places affect how we think and feel.

title: Form Follows Fiasco: Why Modern Architecture Hasn’t Worked
why: A modernist critic’s honest list of modernism’s failures.

title: From Bauhaus to Our House
why: A funny, unfair attack on glass boxes and the people who built them.

title: Architecture: The Natural and the Manmade
why: Scully on how buildings answer the landscape, from Greek temples to Wright.

title: The Shingle Style and the Stick Style
why: The American wooden houses that led to Wright, by the great Yale teacher.

title: Learning from the Vernacular
why: Why architects are turning back to vernacular building, with today’s examples.

title: Design Drawing
why: Seeing and drawing from observation, then drawing to design.

title: Interior Design Illustrated
why: Ching’s visual guide to interior space, light, furniture and finishes.

title: Building Structures Illustrated
by: Francis D. K. Ching, Barry Onouye and Douglas Zuberbuhler
why: Structure explained through drawings rather than maths.

title: Green Building Illustrated
by: Francis D. K. Ching and Ian M. Shapiro
why: Energy, water, materials and site, shown in Ching’s drawings.

title: Architectural Drawing: A Visual Compendium of Types and Methods
why: Every kind of architectural drawing, with many examples from real projects.

title: Drawing Architecture
why: Two hundred and fifty drawings from two thousand years, from plans on clay to digital renderings.

title: Rendering in Pen and Ink
why: The classic pen-and-ink manual, still used for hatching and texture.

title: Understanding Architecture Through Drawing
why: How to use sketching to analyse buildings and cities.
